features.headline: Commanders keep NFC East hopes alive with win over Giants
features.desc: New York couldn't close out a win against Washington, giving up a late touchdown drive. Its division lead is now shrinking.
body: EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J. — The Washington Commanders might have saved their season Thursday night. If nothing else, the Commanders extended the belief that they can contend for the NFC East title.

Washington's comeback 24-21 win against the New York Giants improved its record to 3-5-1. Now, the Commanders are two games behind New York while owning the tiebreaker. They have more work to do to climb back into the race, but the win staved off questions about Dan Quinn's coaching future.

If they had lost Thursday, they would have been all but eliminated — and Quinn's job security would have become a primary topic considering they entered the game 7-17-1 since the start of last season.
It was the first time Washington won by scoring a touchdown on its final drive. The Commanders had been 1-3-1 in games decided by a touchdown or less before Thursday.
Here are the most important things to know for both teams:
What to make of Daniels' performance: Jayden Daniels overcame his first two interceptions of the season and delivered when Washington needed him most.
His strength has been shaking off bad plays, and after consecutive series ended with picks in the fourth quarter, he led the go-ahead touchdown drive — with a 32-yard touchdown pass to Stefon Diggs.
Daniels had been highly efficient prior to that pass. He has gotten better at keeping his eyes downfield, which resulted in one play for 30 yards.

Trend to watch: Washington's defense has forced six turnovers in its past three games combined. The Commanders now have 14 takeaways this season, but none was bigger than corner Rasul Douglas' interception to end the Giants' final possession.

features.headline: How Cubs' Pete Crow-Armstrong became unanimous NL MVP
features.desc: The Cubs' star center fielder hit another level midway through the 2026 season. Here's what shaped PCA's superstar turn.
body: It's easy to forget that Pete Crow-Armstrong was having a quiet first six weeks of the 2026 MLB season after signing a six-year, $115 million contract extension a few months earlier.

The moment that turned the Chicago Cubs center fielder into a runaway favorite for National League MVP honors — and eventual unanimous winner — didn't come until mid-May, in a matchup against the Atlanta Braves and 2024 Cy Young winner Chris Sale.

Crow-Armstrong's defense, as usual, had been outstanding. But while batting ninth in the order during the early portion of the year, he had yet to find his groove at the plate and was batting just.238 with a.679 OPS.
Cubs hitting coach John Mallee attempted a "we have nothing to lose moment" against the nasty left-hander. The Cubs decided to move the lefty-hitting Crow-Armstrong closer to the plate.
"You're either going to get hit or the ball's going forward," Mallee recalled saying to Crow-Armstrong going into the game. "There's only two options because you're standing on top of the plate now."
It was similar to what former Cubs star Anthony Rizzo tried years earlier under Mallee's tutelage.

Back then, when Mallee expressed concern for Rizzo's health — as his hit by pitch totals increased — the former All-Star first baseman famously reminded Mallee that he had survived cancer so he wasn't much afraid of a baseball.
Crow-Armstrong decided he was up for the challenge after talking to Rizzo about it. He wanted to get on base more. Getting hit was one way.

Crow-Armstrong didn't get hit, but he did go 1-for-2 off Sale that day. He turned on a 97 mph pitch for a single in the second then grounded out on a 3-1 count in the fifth. They were not headline generating plays, but they were the genesis for the months filled with such moments ahead.

features.headline: Who has won the MLB MVP Award? All-time winners list
features.desc: MLB's MVP Award is given to top players in the American League and National League. Take a look at the all-time winners list now.
body: There are two MVPs in Major League Baseball each year — one in the American League and one in the National League. Since 1931, the Baseball Writers' Association of America has voted for the MVPs at the end of the regular season and before the start of the postseason.
The award began in 1911 as the Chalmers Award, honoring the "most important and useful player to the club and to the league." That award was discontinued in 1914.

From 1922 to 1928 in the AL and from 1924 to 1929 in the NL, the League Award was presented to "the baseball player who is of the greatest all-around service to his club." Prior winners were not eligible to win the award again during that time.

In 2026, Yordan Alvarez of the Houston Astros won MVP for the American League, the 3rd Astros player to win the award after Jose Altuve in 2017 and Jeff Bagwell in 1994. Pete Crow-Armstrong of the Chicago Cubs won for the National League, the first Cubs player to win it since Kris Bryant in 2016.
Take a look at all-time AL and NL MVP award winners below:
2026: Yordan Alvarez (AL), Pete Crow-Armstrong (NL)
2023: Shohei Ohtani (AL), Ronald Acuna Jr. (NL)
2022: Aaron Judge (AL), Paul Goldschmidt (NL)
2018: Mookie Betts (AL), Christian Yelich (NL)
2017: Jose Altuve (AL), Giancarlo Stanton (NL)
2013: Miguel Cabrera (AL), Andrew McCutchen (NL)
2008: Dustin Pedroia (AL), Albert Pujols (NL)
2007: Alex Rodriguez (AL), Jimmy Rollins (NL)
2005: Alex Rodriguez (AL), Albert Pujols (NL)
2004: Vladimir Guerrero (AL), Barry Bonds (NL)
1999: Iván Rodríguez (AL), Chipper Jones (NL)

features.headline: 2026 MLB Awards: Results, analysis on MVP, Cy Young, more
features.desc: Baseball's best players and managers of 2026 collected their hardware this week.
body: That's a wrap on awards week, closing the books on the 2026 MLB season.
The baseball offseason has felt pretty normal so far if you can put the overhanging labor negotiations out of your mind.
Some of that normalcy comes from the gradual easing into the initial phases of the hot stove season — contract options, roster maneuvering, free agency filing — that point toward next season.

That's administrative stuff, though, and not as fun as the parade in Milwaukee — or this week, when MLB handed out its major awards, featuring the newest honor being handed out by the Baseball Writers' Association of America: the first ever Reliever of the Year Award.
We break down all the major award winners below, culminating in the grand finale on Thursday: the Most Valuable Player Award.
MVP | Cy Young | Reliever of the Year Rookie of the Year | Manager of the Year

Final tally: Alvarez 420 (30 first-place votes, unanimous), Junior Caminero 267, Bobby Witt Jr. 188, Cam Schlittler 181, Pete Alonso 144, Miguel Vargas 129, Kevin McGonigle 109, Randy Arozarena 95, Ben Rice 92, Willson Contreras 67, Dylan Cease 20, Wilyer Abreu 17, Parker Messick 10, Dillon Dingler 7, Steven Kwan 5, Munetaka Murakami 5, Ceddanne Rafaela 4, Ezequiel Duran 3, Drew Rasmussen 3, Isaac Paredes 2, Cade Smith 2
Takeaway: Alvarez becomes the second player who was primarily a designated hitter to win an MVP award, following Shohei Ohtani in 2024 (the only one of his MVP awards he won when he wasn't pitching).
To win this honor, which is meant to recognize the overall value of a player's contribution, a DH has to really separate himself. Alvarez did that and so much more.

features.headline: From Ballon d'Or hopes to Real Madrid bench: Should Liverpool re-sign Trent Alexander-Arnold?
features.desc: Trent Alexander-Arnold's dream move to Real Madrid is turning into a nightmare, but would Liverpool take him back? And would he want to return?
body: It was two years ago that Trent Alexander-Arnold sat down at Liverpool's AXA Training Centre and made the admission that would signal the beginning of the end of his Anfield career.

During an interview with Sky Sports, the defender was asked which dream he would most like to realize: would he rather captain Liverpool, win another Champions League title, win a trophy with England, or win the Ballon d'Or? Surprisingly, he settled on the latter option.
"I believe I can," Alexander-Arnold said. "I want to be the first full back to ever do it."
In a world where footballers — whether sincerely or not — are often quick to downplay the importance of individual accolades versus team success, it was a bold choice.

Six months later, Alexander-Arnold announced he would be leaving his boyhood club to join Real Madrid, who paid Liverpool €12 million so the right back would be available to feature at the FIFA Club World Cup ahead of his contract expiring that summer.

Madrid's desire to expedite the start of Alexander-Arnold's journey at the club was a reflection of how keen the Spanish giants were on his signing. Nearly 18 months on, though, and his career has stalled.

Across his time in Madrid so far, the 28-year-old has started just 18 out of a possible 50 LaLiga games. Injuries have played a part, as has the significant managerial churn at the Bernabeu, but it increasingly feels like the defender's dream move is turning into a nightmare.
Jose Mourinho's appointment as head coach in July has further complicated matters.
